Thanks Marissa — this looks right. A couple clarifications from our side:

- Target SLOs: our product team is aiming for p95 <= 200ms for short answers (<=512 tokens total). For longer analyses (1k-8k output tokens) we expect p95 <= 2s, p50 <= 900ms. Is that achievable with a 16k/32k context?
- Token distributions: avg input ~1,200 tokens (multi-doc), 95th ~4,500. Output avg ~300 tokens, 95th ~3,000.
- Concurrency: steady-state 15–25 rps, but during reporting windows we see spikes to 60 rps for a few minutes.
- Streaming: we need token-level streaming to show partial results in the UI; final-only streaming is not sufficient.

Please confirm whether maintaining token-level streaming with 32k contexts increases tail latency significantly, and whether you recommend different instance types or Dedicated config for that pattern. Also share the mutual action plan to get the trial provisioned.

Alex — great detail, thanks. Quick answers and recommendations:

- Short answers (<=512 tokens): p95 <= 200ms is achievable on our Dedicated high-throughput tier with modest batching disabled for latency-sensitive routes. We typically size for ~1.2x your p95 headroom.

- Long outputs (1k–8k): p95 <= 2s is achievable in many cases but depends on two factors: context window size and streaming model behavior. Longer outputs push more work per request and increase memory footprint; on a 16k/32k context we see ~10–40% higher per-token latency depending on model architecture and KV cache locality.

- Streaming with 32k context: token-by-token streaming is supported, but tail latency can increase because of larger KV cache management and OS-level memory pressure when working set exceeds per-GPU L2 cache. Our recommendation:
  - Use streaming for UI responsiveness, but enable prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts to reduce recomputation.
  - For spikes, provision a Dedicated pool with modest headroom (50–100% burst capacity) or enable autoscale with fast warm-up.

- Instance recommendation: for 15–60 rps with your token sizes, start with our Dedicated m-highmem (8 x A100-style GPUs equivalent) or dedicated mixed nodes tuned for long-context models. We'll size exactly after we run the perf sweep.

- Cost/latency tradeoffs between 8k/32k: see spreadsheet — rough rule: moving from 8k -> 32k increases per-token latency by ~15–35% and VRAM needs by ~2–3x, which impacts packing and effective throughput. If your 95th input is 4.5k and outputs are sometimes 3k, 16k mode may be the best balance.

Next steps / Mutual action plan:
1) Neha to run a 1-hour perf sweep against a sample corpus of your prompts (can be done tomorrow).
2) We provision 3-day Dedicated eval (m-highmem) with streaming enabled.
3) Collect p50/p95 telemetry, then iterate on batching/cache params.

I'll attach the SLO matrix and a quick KV-cache diagram (attached). If all good, can Neha book the perf sweep for tomorrow 10:00–11:00 PT?

Hi Alex — copying some technical detail so you're set for the perf sweep: 

Quick checklist we need from you before the run:
- Representative prompt set (zipped) and a 1-minute peak-simulated qps trace (CSV) — helps reproduce spikes.
- Flag whether prompts are mostly unique or have repeated prefixes (helps caching).
- Confirm whether you need strict end-to-end p95 (network+infra+inference) or inference-only p95.

Technical notes:
- Streaming: we stream tokens as they are generated. For long contexts, we suggest enabling incremental KV eviction and small emission buffer (2–4 tokens) to keep UI latency low while avoiding excessive syscalls.
- Concurrency: Our runtime supports continuous batching — for latency-critical routes we can set max-batch-size=1 and enable immediate dispatch; but throughput will drop. For your mixed profile, we'll use adaptive batching with a target latency cap.
- Measurement: we'll provide per-token histograms, p50/p95/p99 for prefill and decode phases, and end-to-end latency including network for your testers.

I can run the sweep tomorrow at 10:00 PT if you can share the prompt set and qps trace by EOD today. If you'd prefer, we can start with a small dry-run (100 requests) to validate telemetry.

Thanks — Neha
